data.title: Trump to hold one-on-one talks with Putin on the sidelines of Asia summit
data.description:
Trump administration

Trump to hold one-on-one with Putin on the sidelines of Asia summit

A U.S. official confirmed that the two leaders would hold a bilateral meeting despite indications from White House officials that Trump and Putin would not meet separately.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Nov. 18, 2026, 10:39 AM EST / Updated Nov. 18, 2026, 11:08 AM EST
By Monica Alba and Megan Brand

President Donald Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, a U.S. official confirmed, marking the leaders’ first in-person meeting in over a year.

The bilateral meeting was not initially on Trump’s schedule for his Asia trip. The president was already scheduled to hold a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, where the leaders plan to discuss nuclear disarmament, the Iran war, trade and, Trump said Monday, Russia’s war with Ukraine.

The Kremlin had said ahead of the U.S.’ confirmation that the two leaders would be meeting one-on-one.

The White House has not released information about the agenda for the bilateral meeting, which comes as major attacks continue in the Ukraine war with no end in sight. Trump’s meetings with the leaders of China and Russia — both U.S. adversaries — marks his administration’s continued shift away from traditional alliances and unconventional approach to diplomacy.

A senior U.S. official previously told reporters that while the president intended to discuss Iran with Xi and Putin during their trilateral meeting, he did not plan to focus on the war in Ukraine. The official said last week that “it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there” with China.

Trump and Putin previously met face-to-face in Alaska in August 2025. That summit ended without an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, something Trump has been pursuing since he began his second term.

Trump continued to express optimism about ending the war after the in-person meeting in Alaska did not lead to any ceasefire or breakthrough.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said he believed Putin was “backing down a little bit” in the war in Ukraine.

Russia, however, has continued striking Ukraine with missiles and drones in the lead up to the meeting. Separately, on Tuesday, Ukraine damaged a key bridge that links the occupied Crimean Peninsula with Russia.

data.title: DHS chief defends football trip as Congress presses him over nationwide ground stop
data.description:
Mullin, appearing before Congress, defends his flight to LSU-Texas game after nationwide ground stop

REBECCA SANTANA
Updated Wed, November 18, 2026 at 12:01 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended before a House committee Wednesday his flight to a weekend LSU-Texas football game as travelers across the U.S. were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights, saying canceling it could have caused confusion.

Mullin spoke at a congressional hearing about threats facing the country at a time of looming questions over cyber infrastructure, the future of immigration enforcement and his decision to fly to the college football game.

The hearing in front of the House Homeland Security Committee is a standard yearly opportunity for members of Congress to grill top administration officials over national security threats. But it comes as the U.S. has faced a series of cyber and technology problems that have left Americans feeling vulnerable.

Advertisement

The hearing is also the first opportunity for Democrats after their midterm drubbing of Republicans to grill the Cabinet official who is key to President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. Two others facing questioning are FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and the Trump administration's national intelligence director, Jay Clayton.

Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling

The secretary has faced scrutiny over his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday to watch the LSU-Texas game.

Mullin's flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.

On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.

Mullin said the trip had been planned for weeks so that he could take his nieces to the game and that there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.

"If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we're not even willing to fly," Mullin said.

Mullin had said Tuesday and reiterated Wednesday that he is required to fly on government planes and that he personally paid for the trip.

Mullin defends ground stop response

Mullin, whose department includes the agency tasked with protecting the country's cyber infrastructure, was front and center in the Republican administration's response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.

The Trump administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration's telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.

At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn't giving the American public clear answers.

"We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn't have one single incident. That in itself is a great success," Mullin said.

During a news conference Friday with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy at the White House, he pushed for more funding for the aging air traffic control system while also assuring the public that the government was not seeing any signs of a deliberate cyberattack.

The Trump administration has been attempting to offer reassurances about a spate of outages over the last week that have affected everything from Microsoft and the Federal Aviation Administration to the banking industry, United Airlines and a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.

Top Trump administration national security officials have said there was no indication that the events are related or attributable to a cyberattack or hostile activity.

Clayton told the committee Wednesday that the outages are "not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack." Instead, they appear to be "separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes."

Mullin's sprawling Department of Homeland Security also includes an agency designed to play a central role in the federal government's response to cyber incidents. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.

But CISA has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump's original pick to lead the agency withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it languished for months in the Senate.

CISA also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the federal government.

Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny

Mullin, whose department includes Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, faced questions over the Republican president's immigration agenda at a time when Democrats are vowing rigorous oversight of everything from immigration detention contracts to the use of force by ICE officers.

Trump has indicated he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff, raising questions over how easily compromise could be reached on the issue.

Mullin took over from ousted Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in March after the killing of two American citizen protesters in Minneapolis at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.

Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies across the country.

___

Associated Press writers Eric Tucker in Washington, Mike Catalini in Morrisville, Pennsylvania and Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, contributed to this report.

data.title: Chinese President Xi rolls out the red carpet for Trump as a new trade fight looms
data.description:
In China, Trump is greeted by Xi Jinping and meets with Canada's Mark Carney

Ben Werschkul · Washington Correspondent
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 6:43 AM PST 3 min read
  • NVDA -2.07%
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase

Trading disclosure

The above button links to Coinbase. Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational.

Learn more

Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed President Trump with a rare in-person greeting Wednesday in Shenzhen for the Chinese leg of Trump's Asia trip this week.

The Chinese leader even offered Trump a hug, kicking off a visit expected to be dogged by questions of US changes to semiconductor export controls and the ongoing scandal at Nvidia. Trade talks with China and Canada are also on the agenda.

The greeting came ahead of two closely watched sit-down meetings Thursday between Trump and Xi on economic issues and another with Russian President Vladimir Putin joining the conversation.

Trump landed in Shenzhen at 4:42 p.m. local time on Wednesday to a red carpet welcome ceremony, a military band playing the Star-Spangled Banner, and a military flyover, according to a pool report.

The pomp mirrored Trump's tarmac greeting for Xi in the United States in September.

Trump also met with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum later on Wednesday. Carney posted on X that the leaders discussed efforts to reach a trade deal and "agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact."

The meeting follows significant trade war escalations that erupted between the US and Canada earlier this fall. Recent weeks have seen a new round of talks aimed at reaching a deal to reduce current duties and avert a threatened 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks, and auto parts, scheduled to take effect in 2027.

In his own stops ahead of the meeting, Carney announced progress toward lessening trade restrictions with China and Mexico and also claimed that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is not a major concern for Trump.

"We have been making progress," Carney said of talks with the US, but that any deal needs to be "in the interest of Canadians."

Sheinbaum posted a photo of her sitting down with Trump and said it had been "a very good meeting."

A day of opening ceremonies

During Wednesday's whirlwind series of stops, Trump and Xi joined a group photo as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) fully kicked off.

Trump crossed paths with Putin at the festivities, shaking hands and exchanging pleasantries with the Russian leader. The president then participated in a banquet before returning to his hotel for the night.

The gathering this week had been set to focus on digital trade and artificial intelligence, but the scandal at Nvidia (NVDA) and potential changes to US semiconductor export rules are hanging over it.

The Trump administration published new proposed export limits as Trump departed Washington, a move that was immediately felt in the region.

The rule aims to limit China's ability to access advanced chips that reside in data centers outside its borders. It was authored by the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council and has now moved one step closer to being enacted.

Trump traveled to China from the Philippines, where he participated in a series of economic meetings and signed a joint statement with Thailand as the two countries look to finalize a trade deal.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

data.title: Peltola wins Alaska Senate race, and it could have implications for Dems in 2028
data.description:
Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate race colored by double Dan Sullivan controversy

Peltola's victory caps off a midterm cycle in which Democrats flipped nine GOP-held Senate seats to secure a sizable majority in the chamber.

Mike Bebernes
Updated Wed, November 18, 2026 at 1:33 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan to flip yet another Senate seat for Democrats.

Updated vote counts released Tuesday night gave Peltola just over 50% of the first-choice ballots, according to the Associated Press, allowing her to secure victory without having to rely on any second-choice ballots under the state's ranked-choice voting system. 

Peltola's victory comes after weeks of controversy, accusations and legal wrangling stemming from the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan — an unaffiliated candidate who happens to share a name with the incumbent Republican senator — on the ballot.

Advertisement

Alaska's race was the last undecided Senate contest of the midterm cycle, which saw Democrats flip both chambers of Congress with substantial majorities. Peltola is the ninth Democrat to flip a GOP-held Senate seat this year. 

And she is the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Alaska since 2008.

Double Dan drama

Alaska's Senate race came to dominate headlines in the weeks before Election Day when the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit in federal court to block certification of the election results if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan lost by a narrow margin, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan launched his candidacy with the sole purpose of siphoning away votes from the incumbent Republican.

A few days later, the New York Times published an extensive investigation that appeared to substantiate that allegation, calling it "Democrats' secret effort to stack Alaska's ballot."

Trump, who said he ordered the DOJ to file the suit, later argued on Truth Social that both Peltola and the "fake" Dan Sullivan should be removed from the ballot. 

While having two candidates with the same name on the same ballot is unusual, tactical "ballot stacking" is a relatively common — and largely legal — practice among both parties. A federal judge ultimately dismissed the DOJ's lawsuit, writing that any attempt to determine whether Peltola's win could be directly attributed to voter confusion over the two Dan Sullivans would be "infeasible."

Still, investigations by the DOJ and state law enforcement to determine whether any laws may have been broken in the process of getting the second Dan Sullivan's name on the ballot appear to be ongoing.  

Some Republicans have suggested that they may attempt to block Peltola from being seated in the Senate,but Peltola's victory on first-choice ballots makes it more difficult to argue that she won because of voter confusion. There's also the reality that Democrats will be taking over the Senate in early January, which puts a limited shelf life on any campaign to keep her from formally taking her seat. 

Who is Mary Peltola?

Peltola, 53, was born in Anchorage in 1973, the child of a German-American transplant from Nebraska and a Native Alaskan woman of the Yup'ik people — one of several Indigenous groups in western and southwestern Alaska.

She grew up fishing with her father in Yup'ik and became the captain of her own fishing boat by the age of 14. As an adult, she worked for the Alaska Department of Fish and Game and later served as executive director of the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission. Her lifetime of efforts to protect Alaska's wild fisheries and protect its coastal waters have become a key element of her political identity.

Peltola turned to politics in the late 1990s, when she was elected to a seat in Alaska's House of Representatives, where she served for 10 years. Peltola's pragmatic approach to politics was highlighted in 2010, when she led a write-in campaign that helped Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski win reelection after she lost the GOP primary to a Tea Party conservative.

In 2022, Peltola joined the race for Alaska's lone seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, which had been left vacant after the death of longtime incumbent Rep. Don Young. She defeated former Alaska governor and vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin twice in the span of a few months — first in a special election to finish Young's term, then in a general election contest. Peltola was the first Alaska Native and the first woman to represent Alaska in the House of Representatives.

She lost her seat in the House in 2024 in a close race against Republican Nick Begich.

Peltola has been described as "a little more moderate" than the typical Democrat in the "lower 48," by the executive director of the Alaska Democratic Party. Her main slogan throughout her Senate campaign was "fish, family, freedom" — a nod to Alaska's spirit of independence.

Peltola's emphasis on freedom is reflected in her support for the 2nd Amendment and opposition to laws limiting the rights of transgender people. She has also put heavy emphasis on "fixing the rigged system" in Washington and supports reforms like term limits for members of Congress, banning lawmakers from trading stocks and getting "dark money" out of politics. 

A look to 2028

Peltola's win serves as further proof that a Democrat can win a high-profile statewide race in Alaska. Murkowski, 69, will be up for reelection in 2028. It's unclear whether she intends to run for a fifth full term, but her seat has already been identified as one of the key Senate battlegrounds of the next election cycle. 

There will also be a presidential election in 2028. Alaska has voted for the Republican in every presidential race for the past 60 years, but the state's three electoral votes could be in play if the big swing toward Democrats that was seen in this year's midterms proves to be a longer-term trend.

data.title: Xi and Putin blast Western 'protectionism' and sanctions as Trump lands in China
data.description:
Xi, Putin blast Western 'protectionism' and sanctions as Trump lands in China

By Liz Lee, Laurie Chen and Jarrett Renshaw
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 7:28 AM PST 5 min read
  • NVDA -1.69%
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase

Trading disclosure

The above button links to Coinbase. Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational.

Learn more

By Liz Lee, Laurie Chen and Jarrett Renshaw

SHENZHEN, China, Nov 18 (Reuters) - China's President Xi Jinping on Wednesday pledged to stand up against trade protectionism, but also gave a warm welcome to US President Donald Trump as he arrived ahead of a high-stakes trilateral meeting that will include the Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

Xi greeted Trump at the airport, the first time he had ‌done so with any visiting leader since becoming president, reciprocating his counterpart's gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September when they last met.

Trump's arrival came after Xi and Putin delivered pointed speeches ahead of ‌an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

In his opening address, Xi urged support for what he called "free and open trade," trying to portray his country as a stable partner on the global stage, in contrast with the US, which has raised ​tariffs and taken a volatile approach to foreign policy under Trump.

In his speech, Putin criticised Western sanctions imposed over Russia's war in Ukraine.

At the Shenzhen airport, Xi and Trump briefly hugged and exchanged words before walking to their motorcades.

"China is a country of etiquette and has a tradition of reciprocating courtesy," Xi was quoted as saying by state news agency Xinhua. He added he was looking forward to discussing China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape.

Trump said every meeting with Xi has been "very pleasant," Xinhua reported.

They then joined Putin and other leaders at the APEC summit venue for handshakes, a group photo and banquet.

The three men will meet on the sidelines on Thursday and potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and ‌the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, ⁠AI and nuclear weapons.

The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalised spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.

It has also unnerved some European and Asian capitals, which fear the world's greatest military powers will ⁠disregard their interests.

MESSAGE RESONATES WITH GLOBAL SOUTH

Xi's remarks came after Washington announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, which could further complicate a fragile trade truce with Beijing. China has pledged to retaliate.

"We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment," Xi told an audience of business executives.

Western trade partners have criticised China for running annual trade surpluses exceeding $1 trillion through policies that support ​its ​manufacturing sector at the expense of its consumers.

Beijing says its growth model is appropriate for an economy still catching up with the ​world's richest, but Washington, Brussels and others are concerned about China's supply chain dominance ‌providing the country with geopolitical leverage and say its policies threaten their industries and jobs.

Xi said China will continue to invest in its industrial complex and new technologies. The world's second-largest economy will lower tariffs and further open up its markets, while standing up against protectionism and unilateralism, he added.

His "message is likely to resonate with many Global South countries and reinforces Beijing's effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group.

Trump's trip to Asia is his first since his Republican Party's defeat in midterm elections this month, while allegations involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy add to the tension.

COLD RECEPTION FOR TAKAICHI

Leaders from Australia, Canada, South Korea and others were met by dancers and soldiers hoisting rifles, but Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi landed without any welcoming ceremony.

Her visit to China comes amid a rift between Beijing and Tokyo that ‌began a year ago after she said Japan could deploy its military if a Chinese move on Taiwan also threatened its territory.

On ​Tuesday, Taiwan and Japan flagged incursions by Russian aircraft into their airspace.

Putin, who was speaking after Ukraine crippled the vital Kerch road bridge ​linking Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war, followed Xi on stage with a ​speech that described Western powers as "former hegemons."

He said Europe was in a "humiliating decline" and anti-Russian sanctions imposed after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired.

"Experience has shown that the traditional tools ‌of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, having lost ​much of their intimidating power," Putin said.

"While sanctions, tariffs, and ​export restrictions may still exert a certain deterrent effect, they are incapable of halting growth—let alone crushing the economies of competitors."

In Manila, Trump vowed to deepen defence cooperation with the Philippines, amid its growing friction with Beijing over disputed features in the South China Sea. Earlier, he floated the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, but that has not been confirmed.

The Kremlin this week dismissed comparisons ​with the Yalta Conference as "games of political scientists," but said the meeting will have ‌a major impact on global affairs. Beijing said the trilateral will promote world peace.

Putin described the world as "turbulent" but said disagreements can be addressed by "sitting at the table."

"I therefore expect big potential ​benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting," he said.

(Reporting by Liz Lee, Laurie Chen, Trevor Hunnicutt and Ju-Min Park in Shenzhen, Jekaterīna Golubkova in Tokyo, Farah Master in Hong Kong, and Shi Bu ​in Beijing; Writing by Marius Zaharia; editing by David Brunnstrom, Christian Schmollinger, Kate Mayberry, Saad Sayeed and Chizu Nomiyama )

data.title: White House pulls Trump's pick to lead FDA as Republican support falters
data.description:
White House pulls FDA nominee Heidi Overton after wavering support from Senate Republicans

MATTHEW PERRONE
Updated Wed, November 18, 2026 at 12:40 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Tuesday it has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid growing indications she didn't have the votes needed to win Senate confirmation.

Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA after a tumultous year under Trump's first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary.

But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his unsupported claims about the dangers of childhood vaccines.

Advertisement

Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier in the day he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday.

Cassidy had previously called Overton's support for Trump's plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot— "almost disqualifying." And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to push back against Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic.

To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on chamber floor.

Republicans are racing to try to confirm all of Trump's current nominees before they hand over power to Senate Democrats in January.

data.title: Are all of these outages a coincidence — or a glimpse of our AI future?
data.description:
1. Tech
  2. General

Are all of these outages a coincidence — or a glimpse of our AI future?

First Microsoft. Then the FAA. Now the banks, and the NSA, and Apple iCloud. Our systems are failing, seemingly all at once, while big tech continues to hype up AI.

Andrew Romano
Reporter
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 9:00 PM UTC
Add to Preferred Sources
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 9:00 PM UTC

It was bad enough when Microsoft Outlook crashed last Thursday, cutting off email for millions of global users. It was worse the following day when a sudden air-traffic-control glitch triggered a nationwide FAA ground stop, stranding passengers amid thousands of delayed or cancelled flights. 

By the time Monday rolled around and customers of most major banks, including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo, started losing online access to their accounts — as did Apple iCloud users on Tuesday — it was hard not to "wonder," as one cable-news anchor put it: "Is this all coincidental or is there something behind it?"

More to the point, it was hard not to wonder if AI was to blame. "There's a lot of weird stuff going on," traveler Chuck Amasio, 68, told the Associated Press. (Systems at United Airlines and at the National Security Agency also went down earlier this week.) "It makes one think."

Advertisement
Advertisement

While officials insist, for now, that artificial intelligence — or "super intelligence," as the Trump administration has taken to calling it — was not involved in any of these outages, no less of an authority than Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin went on TV Monday night and speculated that… maybe it was? 

"So I started talking to the tech industry and one guy that's very smart with tech, he asked not to mention his name — no, it's not Elon — so let me just put that out," Mullin told Fox News. "So I said, 'What could be causing all these separate outages?' And he says, 'I believe that it's the SI.'" 

MULLIN ON OUTAGES: I talked to one guy in the tech industry, he asked not to mention his name, it's not Elon. I asked, what could be causing these outages? He said I believe it's SI, because these programs aren't designed to work as fast as SI is. 

So when they put in a program… pic.twitter.com/aFwWcVfcm3

— Acyn (@Acyn) November 17, 2026

Either way, experts predict — and have been predicting for months — that it's only a matter of time before rogue AI agents or malicious, AI-powered actors do disrupt society in precisely the way its been disrupted over the last six days: by toppling the tightly interwoven online systems (business, banking, travel, cloud services and so on) that we can't function without. 

In that sense, this destabilizing moment — the inconvenience, the confusion, the creeping sense that "everything is broken" — has served, they say, as a harbinger of things to come. 

A summer of rogue AI incidents

AI isn't just chatbots at this point. It's also "agents" — bots whose whole purpose is to learn tasks other than chatting, and to do those tasks autonomously.

Advertisement
Advertisement

Behind the scenes, frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are constantly training their AI agents to act in new, ever-more-complex ways. Then they test how advanced the agents become by giving them a goal and setting them loose in testing environments (with a few guardrails) to see what they can accomplish. 

But if we've learned anything about AI agents in recent months, it's that they don't always behave as expected. From May to July, a swarm of OpenAI agents — and "swarm" is how the agents referred to themselves — first learned how to communicate and coordinate within the nooks and crannies of OpenAI's own infrastructure. Leaving notes for each other with tips on how to hack their way out and get data they weren't supposed to have, they then actually did just that: broke out of their isolated test environment, accessed the open internet and cheated on their assignment by hacking into another company called Hugging Face. The agents even tried to cover their tracks. At the time, OpenAI didn't realize any of this was happening. 

Since then, barely a week has gone by without similar revelations about AI agents "going rogue." This is one of the biggest problems with AI right now: keeping cutting-edge models "aligned" with human intentions and values. In September, OpenAI scrapped plans to launch its GPT-6.1 Astra model because it "showed higher levels of deception"; the following month, the company admitted that one of its agents had turned off its own safety monitoring, then denied it had done so. 

At this point, even many skeptics seem to agree that the smarter AI gets, the harder alignment will become. They also tend to worry that continuing to lay the groundwork for superintelligent AI is just asking for trouble (even if we don't know exactly what form that trouble will take). 

Advertisement
Advertisement

Yet instead of slowing down, the major AI companies — with IPOs on the horizon — seem to be hurtling toward something called "recursive self-improvement." That's the industry term for letting the models automate more and more of their own development until they effectively create the next model on their own.

"Since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned over the summer. "Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems." 

From there, it isn't much of a stretch to imagine hackers weaponizing AI to cause widespread outages — or AI just doing the job itself. 

"It's easy to dismiss [the Hugging Face] incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage," Amodei wrote. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails."

Are aging systems struggling to keep up with AI?

To be clear, this particular version of the future does not seem to have arrived (yet). Authorities have emphasized, for instance, that none of the recent outrages appear to be cyberattacks. "I can tell you, with 98% certainty, we're not seeing the cyberattack," Mullin said Monday night on Fox News. "No one is out there taking claims for it. We're not seeing the traffic. We're not seeing the footprints going in, we're not seeing the footprints going out."

Advertisement
Advertisement

Instead, the FAA has said that its ground stop — which followed the nationwide rollout of a new $875 million artificial intelligence tool designed to help air-traffic controllers avoid delays — was the result of a faulty component or an installation error by a government contractor during a modernization project. Microsoft has said that its outage was caused by a dormant software bug that was introduced during a recent "network capacity upgrade" and had lingered undetected since July. And Chase characterized its service disruption as "a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems."

But there's a possible AI through-line regardless. 

"What we are seeing, and frankly I'd expect to see more of it, are service disruptions coming from updating and modernizing legacy systems," U.S. national cyber director Sean Cairncross told Semafor's Ashley Gold when she asked whether the recent outages were related. "This is something that's happening in real time, and at the end of the day, we're going to have to go through this to get systems where they need to be. The industry's known this for a while, it's just that it's manifesting."

Some experts suspect this "modernization" is "manifesting" right now — across multiple sectors — in response to (and possibly with the assistance of) rapidly advancing AI. And our systems are now so concentrated and connected that when one piece of critical infrastructure fails, "it fails at national scale," as a tech analyst told USA Today. 

Advertisement
Advertisement

Setting aside the idea of "AI attacks," Peter Wildeford of the AI Policy Network wrote Tuesday on social media that his "more normal guess is that because there have been a lot of AI-discovered cyber vulnerabilities (including lots probably not yet disclosed), companies across all industries are having to do a lot of patches and upgrades, probably faster than usual."

"Such upgrades can sometimes go wrong, causing outages," Wildeford added. 

Mullin hinted at a similar explanation on Fox News. According to his unnamed tech industry source, "these programs aren't designed to work as fast as [AI] is" — and if the upgrades themselves rely on AI, problems could compound.

"When they put in a program that's able to write codes and it goes in and self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself it's like doing a change order on a house," Mullin mused. "When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing. It's a ripple effect. And it causes the systems to be over[run]." 

Advertisement
Advertisement

"That was a conversation I had today," he concluded. "That kind of makes sense to me." 

Whether the homeland security secretary is right — or just conjecturing live, on national television — remains to be seen. As "weird" as the last few days have been, journalist Derek Thompson wrote on Tuesday, we "still can't rule out the possibility that everything breaking at once has been a string of coincidences that has nothing to do with AI." 

What seems less likely, however, is that we'll also be able to rule out that possibility the next time this happens. And the next time. And the time after that.

data.title: U.S. strikes Iranian missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz
data.description:
US, Iran exchange fire despite talks with mediators

By Nayera Abdallah, Jana Choukeir and Phil Stewart
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 8:37 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Nayera Abdallah, Jana Choukeir and Phil Stewart

DUBAI, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The US and Iran exchanged fire on Tuesday, with the US striking an Iranian missile launch site after Iran said it targeted a US military radar system in Bahrain, despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar.

The latest back-and-forth between the US and Iran ‌was a reminder of difficulties ending nearly nine months of war that have destabilised the Middle East, pushed up global energy prices and fueled US voter anger in November ‌elections that punished President Donald Trump's Republican Party.

Advertisement

A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said US fighter jets fired on a Revolutionary Guards missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz in response to Iran's "aggression targeting ​US personnel and assets." Iranian media, citing an Iranian official, said the US attack did not damage infrastructure.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said earlier on Tuesday they targeted a US military radar system at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base, and warned Bahrain over its alliance with the US and stance towards Shi'ite clergy.

Bahrain, which is home to the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet, said it intercepted the attack and there were no reports of casualties or damage.

Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday for talks aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said.

They coincide with a visit to ‌Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. Oman's Foreign Ministry said he ⁠discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, as well as preventing military escalation, with Oman's foreign minister.

Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before ⁠the war but is now partly blocked by Iran.

Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the strait.

Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he also met Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq and informed him about Iran's diplomatic initiative to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.

RISE IN ATTACKS ON TANKERS

The war has ground to a stalemate, with Trump saying he might ​hold ​off from attacking Iran if the US does not face what he described as provocations from Tehran or the ​Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen.

Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously ‌the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign "to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs" using "baseless allegations."

Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the strait, which is a sticking point in negotiations.

Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of the Omani port city of Khasab.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards and navy said on Tuesday that a ship carrying LNG and two oil tankers ‌had caught fire in the strait. Reuters could not independently verify the reports.

Benchmark Brent crude futures were up 0.4% ​at $92.76 a barrel, much higher than before the war but well below April's wartime peak of $126.41.

IRANIAN WARNING

The war continues to spill ​over into other parts of the Middle East as Iran puts pressure on Washington ​through its Houthi allies, who have carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia and seized areas along the Yemeni coast on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, hoping to squeeze Gulf ‌oil producers.

Tuesday's attack on Bahrain, a Shi'ite-majority country ruled by a Sunni ​Muslim family, followed the sentencing there of 64 people, ​mostly Shi'ite clerics, to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran to undermine the state.

Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the court's ruling on Tuesday and said the accusations were baseless. Tehran has long denied interference in Bahrain's internal affairs.

Iran also fired on Bahrain on Sunday, saying it had targeted a US radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base following what ​it said were hostile US actions.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi ‌said Bahrain had made "three key mistakes," which he listed as "cooperating in the invasion of the Islamic Republic of Iran, remaining within the US security bubble, and encroaching on the ​sanctity of Shi'ite religious authority."

These, "if continued, will jeopardize its survival in the region's new security order," Mohebbi said.

(Additional reporting by Yomna Ehab and Elwely Elwelly, Writing by ​Nayera Abdallah, Aidan Lewis and Phil Stewart; Editing by Ros Russell, Peter Graff, Don Durfee and Rod Nickel)

data.title: Jeffries backs major Medicare changes and universal health coverage for kids
data.description:
Congress

Jeffries endorses lowering Medicare age, adding benefits and universal coverage for kids

“A return to the status quo is not acceptable,” the likely next House speaker says, endorsing a series of new policies including vision, dental and hearing benefits under Medicare.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Nov. 17, 2026, 1:34 PM EST
By Sahil Kapur

WASHINGTON — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is calling for an aggressive health care agenda next year for the new Democratic majorities in Congress.

Jeffries, who is the heavy favorite to become speaker of the House on Jan. 3, said Democrats should use their “historic” House majority and “robust” Senate majority to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand coverage under the program to include benefits for dental, vision and hearing.

He also backed universal health coverage for children.

“We should lower the age of Medicare eligibility. We should expand coverage to include vision, hearing, and dental. And we should cover all the kids in the United States of America,” Jeffries said Tuesday in response to a question from NBC News. “Those are bold actions, meaningful actions, important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage.”

The remarks by Jeffries go significantly further than the pre-election health care agenda he laid out in September, which focused on undoing President Donald Trump’s Medicaid spending cuts and restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired in January.

The Democratic leader reiterated his call for those policies on Tuesday, in addition to funding medical research for pediatric cancer, among other areas. He said Congress must go further, though he didn’t say what age to set Medicare eligibility at.

“Right out of the gate, we will aggressively work on fixing the extraordinary damage that’s been done,” he said. “But we also know, as Democrats, that a return to the status quo is not acceptable. ... As part of our commitment that goes all the way back to FDR and Harry Truman to achieving universal access to health care for the American people.”

Jeffries kept the door open when asked if he favors advancing health care measures in a filibuster-proof “reconciliation” bill that can bypass the Senate’s 60-vote threshold and pass without any Republican support. That would make such a bill more likely to land on Trump’s desk, forcing him to decide whether to sign it into law.

Among other key committee chairs who would be involved in negotiating such a bill, Jeffries mentioned “Bernie Sanders, the OG from Brooklyn,” who will chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.

Sen. Sanders, I-Vt., the leading champion of Medicare for All, said that Jeffries appears to be “essentially supporting the first year” of his Medicare for All proposal, which he said includes a Medicare eligibility age of 55, plus extending benefits and covering all children.

data.title: Apple confirms iCloud outage as users report issues with Apple Pay and other services
data.description:
1. Tech
  2. General
  3. Breaking news

Apple confirms iCloud outage as users report issues with Apple Pay, App Store and other services

Following a string of high-profile online service outages this past week, several Apple services appear to be experiencing issues today.

Dan Thorp-Lancaster
Editor
UpdatedTue, November 17, 2026 at 7:40 PM UTC
Add to Preferred Sources
UpdatedTue, November 17, 2026 at 7:40 PM UTC

Apple appears to be experiencing issues with its online services today, preventing some users from signing into iCloud and other Apple services. According to Downdetector, a site that tracks reports of online service outages, iCloud, Apple Support, Apple Pay, and the App Store are all seeing spikes in reports. Apple's support page currently shows it's having issues with iCloud accounts and sign-ins, along with other services.

According to Downdetector reports, these are the services that saw spikes in outage reports:

  • Apple Support

  • iCloud,

  • Apple Pay

  • App Store

  • Apple Business Manager

  • Apple Music

  • Apple Store

  • Sign In With Apple

  • Apple Card

Advertisement
Advertisement

"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," an Apple spokesperson told us in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible."

In addition to iCloud, Apple's support page also flags that AppleCare on Device, which lets you purchase AppleCare on your phone or tablet, is experiencing an outage. That's alongside Apple Business, Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps and Schoolwork

As of 1:10 p.m. ET, the page also listed the App Store and Apple Music as experiencing an outage. Around 1:41 p.m. ET, the affected services on Downdetector started showing a downward trend in reports, indicating they may be recovering.

Users online reported being signed out of services and unable to sign back in. Others reported being unable to activate new iPhones.

Advertisement
Advertisement

The issues follow a string of outages that have plagued online services over the past week. On Nov. 12, Microsoft Outlook and Teams were knocked out for more than 30 hours due to what Microsoft described as a technical issue. On Nov. 13, a technical issue caused all air traffic across the U.S. to be grounded, leading to thousands of canceled and delayed flights.

On Monday, online services at several major U.S. banks experienced problems for several hours after an issue with JPMorgan Chase's systems. Today, CNN reported that a highly classified communications network used by the National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

This is a developing story …
